summary:
Ivanovo Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and no regional deviation from the federal position has been identified, so the oblast is assessed at the national score. Federal criminal and administrative statutes operate directly in the territory with no local discretion over how they are applied.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender change on official documents took effect. Gender-marker changes on documents remain prohibited, so any police stop, hotel registration or transport identity check can read as a mismatch between a trans visitor's paperwork and presentation.

The propaganda regime carries administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, and repeated offences escalate to criminal prosecution with up to four years' imprisonment. The expanded law reaches any public expression, including material that "justifies" gender transition.

Since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising six to ten under Article 282.2. Foreign nationals who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges; three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, and 81 people were found guilty across 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

Enforcement volume has risen alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night (The Guardian, 17 January 2024).

Official advisories match the legal position. The US State Department rates Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings addressed specifically to LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, with the state able but not willing to provide protection.
tangentialFactors:
The baseline for lesbians, gay men and bisexual visitors differs from that of trans visitors: same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, while same-sex marriage is banned and gender transition is prohibited outright (UK Home Office, June 2025). A trans visitor therefore faces a legal exposure that a cisgender LGB visitor does not.

Enforcement has produced deaths. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Coercion against trans people is documented at family level as well as by the state. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life through 2025, quoting a St Petersburg queer woman who described herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Official asylum machinery treats the risk as group-based. The UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
localsOnly:
Residents carry the same prohibitions as visitors, and in several respects more of them. Same-sex marriage is banned, gender transition is prohibited, gender-marker changes on documents are unavailable, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, leaving no lawful domestic route to legal recognition of a person's gender.

The UK Home Office records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment amounting to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them. That assessment governs UK refugee claims and rests on the position that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, form a particular social group under the refugee convention.

Residents charged under the extremist designation face the same Article 282.2 range as visitors, two to six years for participation and six to ten for organising, alongside administrative liability under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. The 101 convictions logged by Human Rights Watch through 30 June 2025 are overwhelmingly administrative rather than custodial, but at least 20 people moved into criminal proceedings between January 2024 and June 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Ivanovo Oblast-specific enforcement reporting is sourced. Whether any of the 101 extremism-related convictions recorded through 30 June 2025 were issued by courts in this oblast is not established here, and no oblast-level breakdown of propaganda-law cases or fines is available in the inventory.

Local conditions of documentation are unresolved. Sources address the national ban on gender-marker changes but say nothing about how police in Ivanovo Oblast handle a mismatch encountered during identity checks, nor about oblast-level access to the remaining healthcare a trans resident might seek.

The raid, death-in-custody and conversion-therapy cases cited here occurred outside this oblast. Their replication within Ivanovo Oblast is not sourced and should not be assumed from the national figures alone.

The enforcement trend figures reported by Meduza and The Moscow Times are national aggregates. Whether the eighteenfold growth in propaganda-law cases over the past decade has been felt in this oblast proportionally is not documented.

The US and UK advisories named here are foreign-government assessments of Russia as a whole. No government has issued an oblast-specific warning, so the absence of one is not evidence of local tolerance.
